units.title: 1. Embolic versus Thrombotic Stroke
units.guide:
The opening comparison table separates embolic from thrombotic stroke by the tempo of deficit and by recovery, site and vessel size.
Embolic stroke presents with full weakness at onset, rapid recovery of consciousness and cortical findings, multiple lesions at different areas, grey-white matter interphase involvement, hemorrhagic transformation and small-vessel involvement, and the table marks thrombectomy as not useful with a worse prognosis; thrombotic stroke evolves its weakness over 48-72 hours, lacks those rapid recoveries and multifocal features, involves large vessels, and is the one for which thrombectomy is useful with better prognosis.
The note adds that weakness evolving beyond 72 hours suggests bleeding or tumour.

units.title: 2. MCA Stroke Patterns in the UMN Approach
units.guide:
The MCA flowchart splits the approach into three arms, beginning with the lenticulostriate branches from M1, which produce internal capsule findings.
The M2 arm gives variable contralateral weakness with aphasia, separating into a superior division with Broca's aphasia and an inferior division with Wernicke's aphasia without weakness.
The third arm is complete MCA involvement, printed as weakness, hemianopia, hemisensory loss, cortical findings and global aphasia.

units.title: 3. Differential Diagnosis by Lesion Site
units.guide:
The differentials open with internal capsule lesions: dense hemiplegia, hemisensory loss, homonymous hemianopia, a more prominent seventh nerve palsy and an absence of cortical findings.
Brainstem lesions are printed as crossed hemiplegia, with an ipsilateral LMN cranial nerve nuclear palsy plus contralateral weakness.
Spinal cord lesions are the third entry, marked by bilateral involvement with a specific level of lesion.

units.title: 4. Upper Motor Neurons: Definition, Functions and Tracts
units.guide:
Upper motor neurons are descending fibres that merge on the anterior horn cell in the spinal cord and on the cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem.
The corticospinal tract integrates highly skilled fine discrete movements of the distal extremities and supplies lower centres with inhibitory impulses, so a lesion inside the spinal cord gives LMN features at the level and UMN features below it; the extrapyramidal system maintains tone and posture and inhibits proximal and antagonistic muscles.
The fibres included are the pyramidal corticospinal tract, which merges on the AHC, and the extrapyramidal fibres, with the rubrospinal tract in the lateral white matter and the vestibulospinal, tectospinal and reticulospinal tracts in the ventral white matter.

units.title: 5. Corticobulbar Fibres, Facial Palsy and the Motor Homunculus
units.guide:
Corticobulbar fibres merge on the cranial nerve nuclei, and the note divides them into bilateral involvement, which produces pseudobulbar palsy as seen in ALS, and unilateral involvement, which is usually symptomless because of bilateral representation.
The single printed exception is the seventh cranial nerve, whose lower half receives contralateral innervation only, so an internal capsule or cortical lesion gives an UMN seventh nerve palsy; the paired diagrams contrast a supranuclear UMN lesion, with drooping of the angle of the mouth and preserved forehead movement, against a facial nerve nucleus or nerve lesion, with deviation of the angle of the mouth and a Bell's palsy picture.
The motor homunculus places the lower limb with ACA lesions and the upper limb and face with MCA lesions, running from hip, leg, trunk, neck, head, shoulder and arm through the wrist, hand and individual digits to the eye, nose, face, lips, teeth and jaw, tongue and pharynx.

units.title: 6. Pyramidal Tract: Cortical Origin and Capsular Course
units.guide:
The pathway begins in the cortex, with the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus providing pyramidal cells of Betz with the lowest threshold at 30%, premotor and supplementary motor cortex at 30% and the primary sensory cortex at 40%.
Fibres converge on the corona radiata and pass through the internal capsule at the anterior two-thirds of the posterior limb, accompanied by corticonuclear and corticorubral fibres, and then run in the cerebral peduncle and brainstem towards the medullary pyramids, the decussation of pyramids and the lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts to the upper and lower motor neurons and skeletal muscles.

units.title: 7. Midbrain to Cord: Brainstem Levels, Decussation and Segmental Distribution
units.guide:
The midbrain panel labels the superior colliculus, oculomotor nucleus, tectum, tegmentum, crus cerebri as the cerebral peduncle, red nucleus, decussation of the rubrospinal tract, oculomotor nerve, cerebral aqueduct, medial longitudinal fasciculus, lemnisci as sensory, substantia nigra, the middle three-fifths carrying corticospinal and corticonuclear fibres and the frontopontine fibres, with a note that the trochlear nerve is not seen at the superior collicular level.
The fibres then run through the basilar part of the pons and decussate at the pyramidal level in the caudal medulla before entering the spinal cord, where the printed distribution is cervical 50%, thoracic 30% and lumbosacral 30%.

units.title: 8. Clinical Features: The Pyramidal Pattern of Weakness
units.guide:
The clinical features begin with an UMN facial palsy involving the lower half with sparing of the upper half, voluntary fibres for skilled learned actions failing before emotional fibres, and preserved deglutition and articulation.
The upper limb loses shoulder abduction and external rotation, leaving it adducted and internally rotated, loses elbow extension and supination, leaving it flexed and prone, and loses wrist dorsiflexion, leaving the hand palmar flexed.
The lower limb loses hip adduction and flexion, leaving it abducted and externally rotated, loses knee flexion, leaving it extended, and loses ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, leaving the foot plantarflexed and inverted, which produces a circumduction gait.

units.title: 9. Tone: Spasticity versus Rigidity, and the Reflex Root Values
units.guide:
Tone change in a pyramidal lesion is printed as clasp-knife spasticity, and the comparison table separates spasticity as velocity and length dependent, resisting movement in one direction during the initial part, and typed as clasp-knife, from rigidity, which is neither velocity nor length dependent, resists in both directions and is typed as lead-pipe or cog-wheel.
The closing root-value note gives biceps jerk C5-C6, triceps jerk C7, finger flexion C8-T1, knee jerk L3-L4 and ankle jerk S1.
